'''Kathleen Hallisey Rubins''' (born October 14, 1978) is an American microbiologist, the inaugural director of the Trivedi Institute for Space and Global Biomedicine at the [[University of Pittsburgh]],<ref name="TrivediInstitute">{{Cite news |last=Aiken |first=Maddie |date=January 30, 2026 |location=Pittsburgh, PA |title=Pitt sets sights high with new institute for space, biomedicine |url=https://www.post-gazette.com/news/education/2026/01/30/pitt-trivedi-institute-space-health/stories/202601290103 |url-access=subscription |newspaper=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] |id={{ProQuest|3298346996}} |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260130143219/https://www.post-gazette.com/news/education/2026/01/30/pitt-trivedi-institute-space-health/stories/202601290103 |archive-date=January 30, 2026 |access-date=January 30, 2026 }}</ref> and retired [[NASA]] [[astronaut]].<ref name="newclass">{{Cite web |date=June 29, 2009 |title=NASA Selects New Astronauts for Future Space Exploration |url=http://www.nasa.gov/astronauts/ascans2009.html |publisher=[[NASA]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090801162824/http://www.nasa.gov/astronauts/ascans2009.html |archive-date=August 1, 2009 |access-date=June 29, 2009 }}</ref> She became the 60th woman to fly in space when she launched on a Russian [[Soyuz (spacecraft)|Soyuz]] spacecraft to the [[International Space Station]] (ISS) on July 7, 2016.<ref name="collectspace-20160706">{{Cite news |last=Pearlman |first=Robert Z. |author-link=Robert Pearlman |date=July 6, 2016 |title=Station-bound NASA astronaut is the 60th woman to fly into space |url=https://www.collectspace.com/news/news-070616a-astronaut-kate-rubins-60th-woman-space.html |work=[[collectSPACE]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260215110331/https://www.collectspace.com/news/news-070616a-astronaut-kate-rubins-60th-woman-space.html |archive-date=February 15, 2026 |access-date=July 7, 2016 }}</ref> She returned to Earth in [[Kazakhstan]] on October 30, 2016, aboard a Soyuz.<ref name="space.com">{{Cite news |last=Cofield |first=Calla |date=October 30, 2016 |title=Soyuz Space Capsule Lands Safely with Crew of 3 |url=https://www.space.com/34548-space-station-crew-returns-expedition-49.html |work=[[Space.com]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251207134459/https://www.space.com/34548-space-station-crew-returns-expedition-49.html |archive-date=December 7, 2025 |access-date=April 25, 2017 }}</ref> She was a crew member of [[Expedition 48]]/[[Expedition 49|49]] and [[Expedition 63]]/[[Expedition 64|64]] of the ISS.<ref name="space.com"/><ref name="NASA Bio" /> Rubins has spent a total of 300 days, 1 hour, and 31 minutes in space, which is the fourth most days in space by a U.S female astronaut.<ref name="NASA Bio" />

==Biography==
Rubins was born in [[Farmington, Connecticut]], and raised in [[Napa, California]]. She did chores around the house to help her fund a trip to [[United States Space Camp|Space Camp]] in seventh grade. The camp inspired her to take more math and science classes in school. In July 2016, Rubin became the third female Space Camp alumna to fly in space.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.spacecamp.com/social/2019-09-06/meet-tremendous-12-space-camps-astronaut-alumni |title=Meet the Tremendous 12! Space Camp's Astronaut Alumni |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=September 6, 2019 |website=Space Camp |publisher=U.S. Space & Rocket Center |access-date=September 12, 2019 |archive-date=July 28, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728202840/https://www.spacecamp.com/social/2019-09-06/meet-tremendous-12-space-camps-astronaut-alumni }}</ref> Her father, Jim, still resides in Napa and her mother, Ann Hallisey, lives in [[Davis, California]].<ref name="NASA Bio"/>

Kathleen Rubins graduated from [[Vintage High School]] in [[Napa, California]], in 1996. She received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in [[molecular biology]] from the [[University of California, San Diego]], and a [[Ph.D.]] degree in cancer biology from [[Stanford University]] Medical School Biochemistry Department and Microbiology and Immunology Department. She was a member of the Kappa Lambda chapter of the [[Chi Omega]] sorority while attending UC San Diego.

For as long as she can remember, Rubins had always wanted to be an astronaut. Her initial understanding was that she would have to become a fighter pilot first and progress from there, but after getting involved with public health HIV prevention in high school she developed an interest in viruses and microbiology and decided to pursue that first instead. Some of her hobbies include flying airplanes and jumping out of them, scuba diving, and entering triathlons, in which she was a member of the Stanford triathlon team.<ref name="katerubinsinterview">{{Cite web |last=Wright |first=Jerry |date=June 29, 2009 |title=In Their Own Words: Kathleen (Kate) Rubins |url=https://www.nasa.gov/astronauts/2009_rubins.html |publisher=[[NASA]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190322225149/https://www.nasa.gov/astronauts/2009_rubins.html |archive-date=March 22, 2019 |access-date=May 2, 2021 }}</ref>

==Microbiology research==
Rubins conducted her undergraduate research on [[HIV-1]] integration in the Infectious Diseases Laboratory at the [[Salk Institute]] for Biological Studies. She analyzed the mechanism of HIV integration, including several studies of HIV-1 Integrase inhibitors and genome-wide analyses of HIV integration patterns into host genomic DNA. She obtained her Ph.D. from Stanford University and, with the [[U.S. Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases]] and the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]], Rubins (who was responsible for building its underlying [[microarray]]) and colleagues developed the first model of [[smallpox]] infection. She also developed a complete map of the poxvirus [[transcriptome]] and studied virus-host interactions using both in-vitro and animal model systems.

Rubins accepted a Fellow/Principal Investigator position at the [[Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research]] (MIT/Cambridge, Massachusetts) and headed a lab of researchers studying viral diseases that primarily affect Central and West Africa. Work in the Rubins Lab focused on poxviruses and host-pathogen interaction as well as viral mechanisms for regulating host cell [[mRNA]] transcription, translation and decay.<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.jove.com/video/1168/vaccinia-virus-infection-temporal-analysis-virus-gene-expression-part|title=Vaccinia Virus Infection & Temporal Analysis of Virus Gene Expression|journal=Journal of Visualized Experiments|date=April 8, 2009|issue=26|article-number=e1168|doi=10.3791/1168|access-date=March 17, 2013|last1=Yen|first1=Judy|last2=Golan|first2=Ron|last3=Rubins|first3=Kathleen|pmid=19488021|pmc=2791082}}</ref> In addition, she conducted research on transcriptome and genome sequencing of ''[[Ebolavirus]]'', ''[[Marburgvirus]]'', and ''[[Lassa mammarenavirus]]'', and collaborative projects with the U.S. Army to develop therapies for Ebola and Lassa.

Dr. Rubins also conducted research regarding space radiation and its effects on astronauts.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chancellor |first1=Jeffery C. |last2=Blue |first2=Rebecca S. |last3=Cengel |first3=Keith A. |last4=Auñón-Chancellor |first4=Serena M. |author-link4=Serena Auñón-Chancellor |last5=Rubins |first5=Kathleen H. |author-link5=Kathleen Rubins |last6=Katzgraber |first6=Helmut G. |last7=Kennedy |first7=Ann R. |date=February 20, 2018 |orig-date=August 19, 2017 |title=Limitations in predicting the space radiation health risk for exploration astronauts |journal=npj Microgravity |volume=4 |article-number=8 |publisher=[[Springer Nature]] |publication-date=April 3, 2018 |doi=10.1038/s41526-018-0043-2 |doi-access=free |eissn=2373-8065 |pmc=5882936 |pmid=29644336 }}</ref> The authors of this study investigated whether or not the Risk of Exposure-Induced Death (REID) that NASA had accepted was accurate enough. Much of the radiation in space is from ion exposure and solar cycle activity. The authors of the ''Nature'' paper concluded that although there are limitations in estimating the radiation levels that astronauts are exposed to while in space, more research needs to be done on the subject.

Another study that Dr. Rubins was involved with was the life-cycle analysis of a family of viruses including the [[smallpox]] virus.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dower|first1=Ken|last2=Rubins|first2=Kathleen H.|last3=Hensley|first3=Lisa E.|last4=Connor|first4=John H.|date=July 2011|title=Development of Vaccinia Reporter Viruses for Rapid, High Content Analysis of Viral Function at All Stages of Gene Expression|journal=Antiviral Research|volume=91|issue=1|pages=72–80|doi=10.1016/j.antiviral.2011.04.014|issn=0166-3542|pmc=3177160|pmid=21569797}}</ref> The researchers utilized fluorescent protein-based reporters to monitor and analyze the function of the Vaccinia virus. This study was important in starting to work on treatment for diseases like mpox. The [[mpox]] is a zoonotic disease originating from the rainforest around Central and [[West Africa]].<ref name="Monkeypox">{{Cite web|title=Monkeypox|url=https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/monkeypox|access-date=May 2, 2021|website=www.who.int|language=en}}</ref> One can contract mpox when coming in contact with the virus from an animal, human, or any material that has been infected with the virus.<ref>{{Cite web|date=December 18, 2018|title=Transmission {{!}} Monkeypox {{!}} Poxvirus {{!}} CDC|url=https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/transmission.html|access-date=May 3, 2021|website=www.cdc.gov|language=en-us}}</ref> In 2003, there was a small mpox outbreak in the United States, which provided more motivation for the study to be conducted.<ref>{{Cite web|date=December 19, 2018|title=2003 United States Outbreak of Monkeypox {{!}} Monkeypox {{!}} Poxvirus {{!}} CDC|url=https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/outbreak.html|access-date=April 30, 2021|website=www.cdc.gov|language=en-us}}</ref> The results of this study provided useful information for the tracking of viral activity and replication. {{As of|2023|01}}, there is still no cure for mpox, but it can be controlled.<ref name="Monkeypox"/>

Rubins was a part of the research team that investigated the effects of microgravity on RNA isolation and PCR analysis. The experiments occurred between April 19 and May 3, 2017. Operations required the use of the WetLab-2 hardware suite consisting of microgravity-compatible STT (ACT2 or Finger Loop syringe), SPM, bubble-removing Pipette Loader (PL), reaction tube centrifugation rotor and a Cepheid SmartCycler® for thermocycling/fluorescence readout.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Parra|first1=Macarena|last2=Jung|first2=Jimmy|last3=Boone|first3=Travis D.|last4=Tran|first4=Luan|last5=Blaber|first5=Elizabeth A.|last6=Brown|first6=Mark|last7=Chin|first7=Matthew|last8=Chinn|first8=Tori|last9=Cohen|first9=Jacob|last10=Doebler|first10=Robert|last11=Hoang|first11=Dzung|date=September 6, 2017|title=Microgravity validation of a novel system for RNA isolation and multiplex quantitative real time PCR analysis of gene expression on the International Space Station|journal=PLOS ONE|language=en|volume=12|issue=9|article-number=e0183480|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0183480|issn=1932-6203|pmc=5587110|pmid=28877184|bibcode=2017PLoSO..1283480P|doi-access=free}}</ref> This study was conducted while on board the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment performed was one of the first successful ones in the WetLab-2, a research station built for microbiology in space. The results of this study were incredibly valuable for the future of space exploration and analysis of space environment samples.

Rubin is currently a professor of microbiology at the [[University of Pittsburgh]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://triblive.com/news/health-now/new-pitt-institute-looks-to-space-for-insight-on-earthly-illnesses/|title=New Pitt Institute Looks to Space for Insight on Earthly Illnesses|first=Jack|last=Troy|newspaper=Pittsburgh Tribune-Review|date=January 30, 2026|accessdate=January 30, 2026}}</ref> On January 30, 2026, she was announced as the inaugural director of Pitt's Trivedi Institute for Space and Global Biomedicine.<ref name="TrivediInstitute" />

==NASA career==
[[File:First-ever sequencing of DNA in space, performed by Kate Rubins on the ISS. 128f0462 sequencer 1.jpg|thumb|Rubins aboard the ISS with the USB [[Oxford Nanopore Technologies|MinION]] sequencer (lower right) that was used in the first DNA sequencing in space, August 2016]]
Rubins was selected in July 2009 as one of 14 members of [[NASA Astronaut Group 20]]. She graduated from Astronaut Candidate Training, where her training included [[International Space Station]] (ISS) systems, [[Extravehicular activity|Extravehicular Activity]] (EVA), robotics, physiological training, T-38 flight training and water and wilderness survival training.

She became the 60th woman in space when she launched on [[Soyuz MS-01]] in July 2016. She was inspired by learning the constellations with her dad and going to local "star-gazing" gatherings and science museums as early as she could remember as a young child. She had always been fascinated with science and exploring the world.<ref name="NASA Bio">{{Cite web |date=April 2024 |title=Biographical Data - Kathleen (Kate) Rubins (Ph.D.) |url=https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/rubins-k.pdf |publisher=[[NASA]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250204055049/https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/rubins-k.pdf |archive-date=February 4, 2025 |access-date=July 21, 2021 }}</ref><ref name="katerubinsinterview" /><ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/expeditions/future.html|title = Future Expeditions|last = Garcia|first = Mark|website = NASA|date = May 26, 2015|access-date = March 9, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Napa-raised astronaut ready for launch to space station |work=[[Napa Valley Register]] |url=http://napavalleyregister.com/news/local/napa-raised-astronaut-ready-for-launch-to-space-station/article_511c3ce9-41ea-597f-b55e-f65bbd3061f4.html |date=June 1, 2016 |last=Yune |first=Howard |access-date=June 1, 2016}}</ref>

In 2021 and 2022, Rubins participated in the fourth edition of the [[ESA PANGAEA]] field geology training program.<ref>{{Cite web|title=What is Pangaea?|url=https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Human_and_Robotic_Exploration/CAVES_and_Pangaea/What_is_Pangaea|access-date=December 8, 2021|website=www.esa.int|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Kate and the Moon – Caves & pangaea blog|url=https://blogs.esa.int/caves/2021/09/16/kate-and-the-moon/|access-date=December 8, 2021|language=en-US}}</ref> Together with the ESA astronaut [[Andreas Mogensen]], Rubins trained in the Italian Dolomites, Ries Crater in Germany, the volcanic landscapes of Lanzarote, Spain, and the anorthosite outcrops of Lofoten, Norway.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Astronaut training in the land of volcanoes – Caves & pangaea blog|url=https://blogs.esa.int/caves/2021/11/11/astronaut-training-in-the-land-of-volcanoes/|access-date=December 8, 2021|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Geology finale for astronauts on a Moon-like fjord – Caves & pangaea blog |url=https://blogs.esa.int/caves/2022/07/18/geology-finale-for-astronauts-on-a-moon-like-fjord/ |access-date=2024-05-23 |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Expedition 48/49===
Rubins left Earth for the first time on July 7, 2016, on board the new [[Soyuz MS]] spacecraft alongside Russian cosmonaut [[Anatoli Ivanishin]] and [[JAXA]]
astronaut [[Takuya Onishi]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.spacefacts.de/mission/english/soyuz-ms.htm|title=Spacefacts Soyuz MS}}</ref>

In August 2016, Rubins became the first person to [[DNA sequencing|sequence]] [[DNA]] in space. Rubins and the other astronauts were conducting research on how to diagnose an illness, or identify microbes growing in the International Space Station and determine whether or not they represent a health threat.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/news/science/sdut-kate-rubins-DNA-2016aug29-story.html|title=UCSD alumna first to sequence DNA in space|last=Robbins|first=Gary|work=The San Diego Union-Tribune|date=August 29, 2016|access-date=October 26, 2016|archive-date=October 26, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161026232246/http://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/news/science/sdut-kate-rubins-DNA-2016aug29-story.html}}</ref> San Diego graduate, Kate Rubins, used a commercially available machine to sequence mouse, virus and bacteria DNA.<ref name="sandiegout-20160902">{{Cite news |last=Robbins |first=Gary |date=September 2, 2016 |orig-date=August 29, 2016 |title=UCSD alumna first to sequence DNA in space |url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2016/08/29/ucsd-alumna-first-to-sequence-dna-in-space/ |newspaper=[[The San Diego Union-Tribune]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260415204343/https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2016/08/29/ucsd-alumna-first-to-sequence-dna-in-space/ |archive-date=April 15, 2026 |access-date=May 7, 2021 }}</ref> Aboard the ISS, she used a hand-held, [[USB]]-powered [[DNA sequencer]] called the MinION made by [[Oxford Nanopore Technologies]] to determine the [[DNA sequences]] of mouse, ''[[E. coli]]'' bacteria, and [[lambda phage]] virus.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/news/dna_sequencing|title=First DNA Sequencing in Space a Game Changer|last=Gaskill|first=Melissa|work=NASA|date=August 29, 2016|access-date=October 26, 2016|archive-date=November 5, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211105181740/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/news/dna_sequencing/}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.biotechniques.com/news/biotechniquesNews/biotechniques-365181.html|title=DNA Sequencing in the Final Frontier|last=Dance|first=Amber|work=BioTechniques|date=October 19, 2016|access-date=October 26, 2016|archive-date=October 26, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161026232724/http://www.biotechniques.com/news/biotechniquesNews/biotechniques-365181.html}}</ref> It was a part of the Biomolecule Sequencer experiment, the goal of which was "to provide evidence that DNA sequencing in space is possible, which holds the potential to enable the identification of microorganisms, monitor changes in microbes and humans in response to spaceflight, and possibly aid in the detection of DNA-based life elsewhere in the universe."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/news/biomolecule_sequencer|title=Sequencing DNA in the Palm of Your Hand|last=Dunn|first=Andrea|work=NASA|date=September 29, 2015|access-date=October 26, 2016|archive-date=November 14, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211114192518/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/news/biomolecule_sequencer/}}</ref>

During her first stay in space, she also spent 12 hours and 46 minutes outside the station on two separate [[Extravehicular activity|spacewalks]].<ref name="NASA Bio" /> She made these two spacewalks with veteran spacewalker [[Jeffrey Williams (astronaut)|Jeffrey Williams]].<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.spacefacts.de/eva/astronauts/english/rubins_kathleen.htm|title=Kate Rubins EVA Spacefacts}}</ref> During her first spacewalk, Dr. Rubins successfully installed the first International Docking Adapter, which allows U.S. commercial spacecraft to dock.<ref name="NASA Bio" /> On her second spacewalk, Rubins installed new, high definition cameras. Rubins also captured the [[SpaceX Dragon]] commercial resupply spacecraft and sent back experiment samples to Earth.

Rubins returned to Earth on October 30, 2016, after 115 days in space.<ref name="NASA Bio" />

===Expedition 63/64===
[[File:ISS-64 Kate Rubins in front of the 'voting booth'.jpg|thumb|right|Rubins pictured next to the ISS "voting booth", where she cast her [[Voting in space|vote]] for the [[2020 United States presidential election]]]]
Rubins launched on her second mission on October 14, 2020 (her 42nd birthday) with Russian cosmonauts [[Sergey Ryzhikov (cosmonaut)|Sergey Ryzhikov]] and [[Sergey Kud-Sverchkov]] aboard [[Soyuz MS-17]].<ref name="Release 20-060">{{cite web |title=Press Release: NASA Assigns Astronaut Kate Rubins to Expedition 63/64 Space Station Crew |url=https://www.nasa.gov/press-release/nasa-assigns-astronaut-kate-rubins-to-expedition-6364-space-station-crew |website=NASA |date=June 3, 2020 |access-date=June 5, 2020}}</ref> She returned to Earth on April 17, 2021, at 10:55 AM local (Kazakhstan) time, following the launch of [[Soyuz MS-18]].

Rubins was on the ISS at the time of the [[2020 United States elections]] and cast her absentee ballot from the station.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Baird|first=Daniel|date=October 28, 2020|title=How NASA Transmits Votes From the Space Station|url=http://www.nasa.gov/image-feature/goddard/2020/how-nasa-transmits-votes-from-the-space-station|access-date=December 20, 2020|website=NASA}}</ref>

During her second stay in space, she made her third career spacewalk with [[Victor Glover]], and her fourth with [[Soichi Noguchi]] in March 2021.<ref name="Moran-Feb-28">{{cite web|last=Moran|first=Norah|url=https://blogs.nasa.gov/spacestation/2021/02/28/spacewalkers-conclude-todays-spacewalk/|title=Spacewalkers conclude today's spacewalk|date=February 28, 2021|publisher=NASA|access-date=March 1, 2021}}{{PD-notice}}</ref>

==== Research on Expedition 63/64 ====
While on the ISS during her most recent trip, Rubins continued research for the Cardinal Heart experiment which included cancer therapies and heart conditions. [[Micro-g environment|Microgravity]] significantly affects heart tissues that perform work and exert an opposite force to gravity and is known to cause molecular and structural abnormalities in cells and tissues that can lead to disease. The investigation could provide new understanding of similar heart issues on Earth and help identify new treatments.<ref name="nasa-20201210">{{Cite web |last=Keeler |first=Bill |date=December 10, 2012 |title=ISS Daily Summary Report |url=https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/stationreport/2020/12/10/iss-daily-summary-report-12-10-2020/ |publisher=[[NASA]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260330234427/https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/stationreport/2020/12/10/iss-daily-summary-report-12-10-2020/ |archive-date=March 30, 2026 |access-date=May 1, 2021 }}</ref> This study was analyzing the effects of low-gravity on heart muscles. Dr. Rubins and other scientists generated 3D engineered heart tissue. This research could provide important information for heart problems not only for astronauts returning home, but also for any citizen on Earth.

== Awards and honors ==
Rubins has a total of five honors and awards so far in her career. She received Popular Science's Brilliant Ten (2009), National Science Foundation Predoctoral Fellowship (2000), Stanford Graduate Fellowship - Gabilan Fellow (2000), UCSD Emerging Leader of the Year (1998), and Order of Omega Honor Society Scholarship Award (1998).<ref name="NASA Bio"/>
